GOODYEAR OPENS GOODYEAR MOTOR CITY GARAGE RETAIL CONCEPT, CELEBRATES 2026 WOODWARD DREAM CRUISE WITH RARE DOUBLE-BLIMP EVENT
summary: New Goodyear Motor City Garage in Detroit delivers car enthusiast experience around vehicle care Goodyear celebrates Detroit auto performance history since outfitting Henry Ford's 999 race car in 1901
body_text: New Goodyear Motor City Garage in Detroit delivers car enthusiast experience around vehicle care Goodyear celebrates Detroit auto performance history since outfitting Henry Ford's 999 race car in 1901 Goodyear offers Mobile Garage in Detroit — installing tires and servicing cars right in your driveway AKRON, Ohio, and DETROIT , Aug. 3, 2026 / PRNewswire / -- Just in time for the 2026 Woodward Dream Cruise, Goodyear is opening its Goodyear Motor City Garage, its first retail concept store in Detroit. Two Goodyear Blimps will also take to the skies over the Motor City that weekend — the first double-blimp appearance in Detroit in nearly two decades — offering a bird's-eye view of one of the world's largest automotive events, featuring more than 40,000 classic and custom cars and 1.5 million-plus enthusiasts. The Goodyear Motor City Garage will be open to the public during Dream Cruise weekend on Saturday, Aug. 15, at 8 a.m. Located at 3075 East Grand Blvd. in Detroit, this special Goodyear Auto Service Center showcases the company's products, technology and heritage and gives a look at the vision for the future of vehicle care. "Some of the best vehicles in the world have been laying down Goodyear rubber in Detroit since Henry Ford put them on his 999 race car in 1901. From track to tarmac to trail, Goodyear makes tires worth bragging about, and we'll be doing just that during the Woodward Dream Cruise," said Goodyear CEO Mark Stewart. "Whether you're an enthusiast looking for ultra-high performance or just need help picking the best tires to get your SUV through the school pick-up line, we're looking to show you how easy Goodyear can make vehicle care. Detroit's car culture makes it the perfect place to showcase our new retail concept alongside our Mobile Garage service that can install tires and service your vehicle right in your driveway." In addition to the double-blimp appearance, Goodyear will fly a new generation of remote-controlled mini blimps during Dream Cruise festivities. Additional event details, activations, blimp viewing opportunities and schedules will be announced closer to the event on Goodyear's social media channels. The Goodyear Motor City Garage offers tires and service in an enthusiast environment Inspired by destination concepts such as a Starbucks Reserve Roastery or a Nike House of Innovation, the Goodyear Motor City Garage is more than a traditional tire and service location. The space is designed as a gathering spot where enthusiasts can connect with car culture, explore the latest tire technology and engage with Goodyear in a new way. Guests can visit the Goodyear Motor City Garage for the same expert service available at other Goodyear Auto Service locations, including: Tire sales and installation Oil changes Alignments Brake service Battery replacement Free vehicle inspections Preventive maintenance As a tribute to the city that helped shape American car culture, the Goodyear Motor City Garage will showcase a custom, one-of-a-kind Detroit-themed Eagle racing tire. This tire is laser-carved with a love letter to Detroit that celebrates the city's automotive heritage and Goodyear's longstanding connection to the Motor City and its auto enthusiasts. The letter concludes with "We might be from Akron, but we grew up here. Still. Always. Forever." Goodyear displays historic vehicles during Dream Cruise weekend At the Goodyear Motor City Garage during Woodward Dream Cruise weekend, Goodyear will display the famous 1973 Ford Mustang convertible from the opening sequence of "The Mary Tyler Moore Show," courtesy of the Ford Motor Company Heritage Collection. The vehicle is equipped with Goodyear Performance Series F70/14 custom wide-tread tires with raised white letters, a factory-accurate recreation of the original equipment specification. The tires deliver unmistakable vintage performance and period-correct muscle-car presence. Also on display from the General Motors Heritage Center and Archive is the 1977 Pontiac Firebird Trans Am W72 "Bandit." This black-and-gold special edition was inspired by the movie, "Smokey and the Bandit," starring Sally Field and Burt Reynolds. This Trans Am originally was outfitted with Goodyear GR70/15 GM Custom Tread tires. Additional vehicle displays and featured automotive attractions will be announced closer to the event. Goodyear is transforming for today's driver Goodyear has been transforming its business to meet the needs of a rapidly changing automotive landscape. That transformation includes a revamped consumer portfolio with approximately 1,500 new products planned for launch in 2026, a focus on higher-performance and larger rim-size tires, continued investment in manufacturing and modernization efforts across both the Goodyear and Cooper brands. With its global headquarters in Akron, Ohio, Goodyear stands apart as the only major tire manufacturer headquartered in the United States and is focused on becoming the first choice for tires and service. By becoming more consumer-focused, digitally connected and retail-driven, the company is strengthening its position in the premium tire market while making tire buying and automotive services more seamless. The Goodyear Motor City Garage concept store is a real-world example of that vision. About Goodyear Auto Service, Just Tires and Goodyear Mobile Service Goodyear Auto Service and Just Tires stores make car care easy, offering tire sales and installation, alignments, oil changes, brakes, battery replacement and more. Whether you need a quick fix or routine maintenance, our experts help keep your vehicle running and on the road with easy-to-schedule appointments through goodyear.com or by calling the store nearest you. Goodyear also offers a convenient mobile installation service in 28 markets across the country, including Detroit, giving people the option to have their tires installed and serviced wherever they are. Detroit and Goodyear's performance legacy The Woodward Dream Cruise is widely considered the largest one-day automotive event in the world, attracting roughly 1.5 million people and more than 40,000 classic, custom and collector vehicles annually. The Dream Cruise honors the legacy of Detroit automotive engineers and enthusiasts who once tested their vehicles by racing from stoplight to stoplight up and down Woodward Avenue. Goodyear was the original equipment supplier for many of the muscle cars and performance vehicles that helped define that era. Goodyear's history in Detroit stretches back to the earliest days of the automobile. In the early 1900s, when Henry Ford wanted to test his vehicles through racing, one of his first calls was to Goodyear. The company's growth was closely tied to the rise of Detroit and the automakers that transformed the city into the center of the automotive world. Woodward Avenue stretches 27 miles from downtown Detroit to Pontiac and includes America's first concrete-paved mile—where millions of Goodyear tires have left their mark over the years. About The Goodyear Tire & Rubber Company Goodyear is one of the world's largest tire companies. It employs about 63,000 people and manufactures its products in 48 facilities in 19 countries around the world. Its two Innovation Centers in Akron, Ohio, and Colmar-Berg, Luxembourg, strive to develop state-of-the-art products and services that set the technology and performance standard for the industry. For more information about Goodyear and its products, go to www.goodyear.com/corporate CONTACT: KELLY MCGLUMPHY KELLY_MCGLUMPHY@GOODYEAR.COM SOURCE The Goodyear Tire & Rubber Company

title: From Vision to Venture: How Target Supports Emerging Businesses and Founders
summary: Our commitment to developing and uplifting emerging businesses runs deep. Learn how we’re helping them move from vision to venture.
body_text: Founder-led and emerging brands are an important part of Target’s merchandising authority: bringing newness, innovation and distinctive products to our assortment while helping Target anticipate what guests will want next. From industry-leading accelerator programs and supplier engagement to community partnerships and our merchants’ constant search for the next great brand to launch at Target, we’re deeply invested in supporting emerging businesses. Read on to learn how we’re bringing this commitment to life. Accelerating emerging businesses At Target, our merchants are constantly looking for brands and products that bring something new to the Target experience. Emerging brands play an important role in our carefully curated mix of owned, national and emerging brands, helping us introduce guests to fresh ideas, compelling products and founders with distinctive points of view. And when we see potential, Target can offer founders more than a place on shelf. Through retail education, mentorship, merchant connections and opportunities to launch and scale, we help emerging brands navigate what it takes to succeed in mass retail. Discovering what’s next Finding the next great brand starts with creating more ways for founders and Target merchants to connect. Through brand discovery events, Target brings emerging brands and founders together with our teams to showcase innovative products, exchange insights and explore potential pathways to Target. This summer, we hosted over 50 Food & Beverage emerging brands in Minneapolis to showcase their products to Target merchants. For many founders, events like these are an opportunity to earn a place on Target shelves—and take the next step from startup to national brand. We host these events twice per year across categories, allowing our merchants to spend time exploring different brands that we know our guests would love. Preparing founders for retail Another way we find and welcome small businesses to Target? Investing in our leading signature program — Target Takeoff — that helps thousands of small businesses and aspiring entrepreneurs across our product categories.

title: Hormuz Is Choking. Somehow, the Oil Keeps Moving.
summary: Hormuz traffic has plunged, but oil continues moving through alternative routes. Understanding those routes explains why gasoline prices haven’t exploded even higher.
body_text: Hormuz traffic has plunged, but oil continues moving through alternative routes. Understanding those routes explains why gasoline prices haven’t exploded even higher. KEY TAKEAWAYS Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has collapsed. A route that normally carries roughly one-fifth of global oil is operating at only a fraction of its normal activity. Oil has not stopped moving—it has changed routes. Ship-to-ship transfers outside the danger zone and Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline are helping bypass the Strait. Official and independent estimates of Gulf oil flows appear dramatically different. Government figures suggest considerably more oil is escaping the region than vessel-tracking data would seem to indicate. The Strategic Petroleum Reserve is cushioning the disruption. That can help suppress near-term price pressure, but it exchanges current stability for a future replenishment obligation. Lower gasoline prices should not be mistaken for resolution of the underlying problem. The system is functioning because extraordinary workarounds are compensating for a badly impaired shipping route. MY HOT TAKES The price at the gasoline pump is currently a poor measure of stress in the global energy system. Consumers are seeing the result of successful intervention and adaptation rather than an absence of disruption. Markets should pay more attention to inventories and infrastructure than headlines about gasoline prices. The SPR level may ultimately tell investors more about the durability of current conditions than a few cents of movement at the pump. Alternative oil routes demonstrate impressive resilience, but resilience is not the same as excess capacity. Tanker relays and pipelines can buy time without permanently replacing unrestricted access through Hormuz. The disagreement between official flow estimates and independent vessel tracking deserves attention. When observable physical activity and reported aggregate numbers diverge sharply, investors should understand exactly how the figures are being constructed. The most important question is shifting from whether oil can reach the market today to how long these workarounds can remain sustainable. The longer the disruption persists, the more important depleted reserves, transportation costs, insurance, infrastructure limits, and eventual SPR replenishment become. You can quote me: “The number on the sign at the gas station or on TV is never the whole story.” The new OLD thing . Somewhere between when I first turn on my Bloomberg each morning at around 4:00 AM and when I rush out of my apartment to head to the office, at least one stiff espresso is consumed while standing staring at the local NY weather and traffic on broadcast TV. Don’t ask why as I could get far more information from the hot little phone in my pocket. The interesting thing is that I love to watch the traffic report–I don’t drive–but the traffic reporter always reports gas prices in New York, New Jersey, and Connecticut. According to her reporting, the past few days have seen NJ gasoline go below $4! Now that doesn’t exactly jibe with what I am seeing on my Bloomberg screen which shows me the average US retail price tracked by AAA. It also doesn’t jibe with crude oil prices which have been on the climb these past several days since tensions and rhetoric (and even some “unidentified” projectiles hit some ships in the region). My friends, I have been at this for nearly four decades, and if there is one lesson the market refuses to stop teaching me, it is this: the number on the sign at the gas station or on TV is never the whole story. It is the headline. It is the thing your neighbor mentions in the driveway. And this week, that number actually did tick down a few pennies–which, if you stopped reading right there, would sound like good news. Meanwhile, the now-infamous Strait of Hormuz–the artery that normally carries a fifth of the world's oil–saw exactly ten cargo ships cross it since Friday. Both of those facts are true at the same time, and today I want to show you how. Let's start with the number that should stop you cold. Before this war, somewhere north of a hundred ships a day threaded the Strait of Hormuz, carrying close to 20 million barrels of oil. That is not a rounding error in the global energy system–that is one-fifth of everything the world burns, moving through a channel you could practically kick a soccer ball ⚽ across at its narrowest point. Last weekend, ten ships made that crossing. Ten. On Monday, three vessels transited–and not a single one was a crude tanker. This is not a slowdown. A slowdown implies the highway is still open and traffic is just heavier. This is closer to a highway with a checkpoint every hundred yards manned by people who occasionally shoot at you. Nobody is commuting through that willingly. So here is the part that should genuinely surprise you: gas prices did not spike. They eased. The national average sits at $4.06 a gallon today, down slightly from $4.09 a few weeks back. If the main artery for global oil is running at roughly ten percent of normal capacity, why isn't your local Shell station charging you like it's a hostage situation? The answer is that the oil is actually still moving–it is just not moving through the front door anymore. Roughly 150 tankers are currently anchored off the coast of Oman, running what amounts to a floating relay race: one ship loads crude from a Gulf port, sails out through calmer waters, and transfers its cargo ship-to-ship to a second tanker waiting outside the danger zone, which then carries it on to market. One shipping executive called this a "dark trade," which sounds like something out of a heist movie, but is really just insurance math with extra steps. Owners are avoiding the direct run through the Strait because getting shot at tends to void your policy. JPMorgan estimates this relay system alone is currently moving something like 4 million barrels a day–real oil, reaching real refineries, just taking the scenic route. Now, here is where I have to put on my referee stripes, because Washington and the people who actually track ships by satellite are telling two very different stories. The Department of Energy says the seven-day average leaving the Strait is running close to 9 million barrels a day, and that combined with pipeline flows, total volume out of the Gulf region is approaching 15 million barrels a day–with one single day, they claim, exceeding the pre-war average entirely. Independent trackers who watch this stuff for a living–the firms with the satellites and the transponder data, not the podium–are having a hard time making that math work. Their count of actual ship traffic simply doesn't support numbers that large. I'll let you draw your own conclusion about why two sets of very smart people, looking at the same ocean, are seeing two different oceans. I will just note that when the official number and the observable number disagree by this much, the observable number usually wins the argument eventually. It just takes longer to admit it than a press conference does. The other leg of this workaround is Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline–the Petroline, if you want to sound like you know people (I do know people–my friend Peter 😉)--which physically carries oil overland to the Red Sea, sidestepping the Strait entirely. It has a capacity of about 7 million barrels a day and it is, by all accounts, being run hard right now. This is the boring, unglamorous hero of the whole story: no satellites needed to track it, no drama, just steel pipe doing what steel pipe does. Between the shadow relay off Oman and this pipeline grinding away in the background, you start to see how the world is quietly patching a hole in its own energy supply without most people noticing there was ever a hole to patch. But patchwork has a cost, and this is the part of the story nobody's celebrating at the gas pump. While tankers play relay races and pipelines run flat out, the United States has been quietly opening its own spare tank. The Strategic Petroleum Reserve now sits at 298.7 million barrels –the lowest level since 1983–down from 415 million barrels at the start of this year. President Trump authorized the release of 172 million barrels back in March, and the reserve has been paying that bill in installments ever since. For context, the minimum level considered safe to keep the reserve operational is roughly 70 million barrels. We are not near that line today. But we are a lot closer to it than we were in January, and reserves, unlike pipelines, do not refill themselves while you sleep. That's the trade-off nobody put on a bumper sticker. Every barrel the SPR releases to keep prices calm today is a barrel that has to come back eventually, and refilling a reserve is a famously slower, clumsier process than draining one. You can empty a swimming pool with a drain in an afternoon; filling it back up with a garden hose takes all summer. And even once the Strait reopens–and it will, eventually–the reserve doesn't magically top itself off. Somebody has to go buy that oil back, ideally without spiking the very prices the reserve was built to protect against in the first place. Add in the fact that government auditors flagged earlier this year that a meaningful chunk of the reserve's storage infrastructure isn't even fully usable at the moment– aging caverns needing repair, like most things built in the 1970s and asked to still perform in 2026–and you start to understand why "the reserve is doing its job" and "the reserve is fine long-term" are two very different sentences. So where does that leave us this morning? Traffic through the Strait is about as close to zero as a major global shipping lane gets without a sign that says CLOSED. Gas prices ticked down, and that relief is real, but it's being financed by a shadow fleet playing chicken with Iranian patrol boats, a Saudi pipeline running at full tilt, and an American reserve that's been quietly writing checks since March. None of that is free. None of it is permanent. And none of it fixes the actual problem sitting at the bottom of the Persian Gulf. I don't say any of this to scare you into checking oil futures every fifteen minutes. I say it because the calm at the pump right now is borrowed, not earned, and understanding who's fronting the loan is the difference between being surprised later and simply being prepared. Keep an eye on that reserve number. It's a far better crystal ball than the sign outside your gas station. Come to think of it, I am on espresso number two by the time the traffic reporter runs down the numbers. YESTERDAY’S MARKETS The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.5% to close at 53,459.78, the S&P 500 declined 0.5%, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.3%. West Texas Intermediate crude rose 0.6% to $85 a barrel, while Brent crude settled above $90 a barrel. The 10-year Treasury yield closed around 4.69%, and the 30-year Treasury yield topped 5.31%, its highest level in 19 years. Treasuries sold off broadly as investors weighed rising energy costs and long-end yield pressure ahead of a heavy week of retail earnings. title: Best Boutique Hotel Management Software: All-in-One Solution
summary: In this guide, we explore the existing options for boutique hotels in 2026 and how to choose the right one for your property.
body_text: Keeping up with the Joneses on a boutique hotel budget is tricky. The market demands that independent properties offer seamless digital experiences like mobile check-in and instant communication — without losing the human touch. And while tech stacks are a corporate mandate at major hotel chains, they can make or break an independent hotel. Without massive corporate IT resources, choosing software is risky. The right independent hotel management software has the proper level of flexibility and automation to improve operations, guest experience and revenue. In this guide, we’ll explore the existing options for boutique hotels in 2026 and how to choose the right one for your property. Best Boutique Hotel Management Software Key Features Canary AI-powered Guest Management System, Mobile Check-In, Guest Messaging, Dynamic Upsells, AI Voice, Digital Compendium, Smart Checkout, Mobile Key integration, hospitality-specific AI workflows Mews Cloud-based Property Management System (PMS), self-service kiosks, automated payments, housekeeping management, open Application Programming Interface (API) integrations Cloudbeds Property management, channel manager, booking engine, revenue management tools, reporting dashboards Stayntouch Mobile-first PMS, contactless check-in, housekeeping coordination, guest engagement tools Hotelogix Multi-property management, front desk automation, channel management, analytics and reporting RMS Cloud PMS, guest messaging, dynamic pricing, housekeeping automation Little Hotelier PMS designed for small hotels and inns, booking engine, channel manager, front desk management RoomRaccoon PMS, automated upselling, payment processing, housekeeping tools Oracle OPERA Cloud Enterprise-grade PMS, reservations, Customer Relationship Management (CRM) integrations, housekeeping and operations management ThinkReservations PMS for small operations, booking engine, automated guest communication, payment processing, reporting tools Maestro PMS Small property PMS, spa and activity management, guest profiles, multi-property support What Is Boutique Hotel Software? Boutique hotel software is any technology platform that manages independent hotel operations, automates guest interactions and delivers personalized hospitality experiences. Unlike enterprise systems built for large hotel chains, boutique hotel management software focuses on flexibility, ease of use and streamlined workflows for smaller teams. Boutique hotels need specialized technology to easily balance day-to-day operations, including mobile check-in, guest messaging, housekeeping coordination and upselling automation with a high-touch guest experience. For simplicity and to free up staff to concentrate on providing individualized service, many boutique hotels opt for all-in-one solutions that integrate operations with guest engagement. Best Hotel Management Software for Boutique and Independent Hotels A boutique hotel is a curated space where an agile team needs the freedom to pivot on a dime — not click through 20 sub-menus to check in a guest. The best hotel management software gives smaller teams the tools to automate repetitive tasks, streamline workflows and create seamless guest interactions without the complexity of enterprise systems designed for large chains. ‍ Below are the 11 best management software solutions designed to give boutique properties the automation, flexibility, and power to outmaneuver the giants. 1. Canary Canary is an AI-powered Guest Management System built for modern hotels that want to improve operations and elevate the guest experience. The platform combines guest engagement, communication and operational automation tools into a single platform that integrates seamlessly with any PMS. From Mobile Check-In and Smart Checkout to AI Voice and AI Guest Messaging, Canary helps boutique hotels reduce front desk workload while delivering faster, more personalized service and creating the unique guest journeys hotels desire. The platform’s hospitality-specific AI tools automate repetitive guest interactions across voice, text and webchat so staff can focus on high-value, in-person experiences that define boutique hospitality. Pros of Canary: AI-powered guest communication across voice, webchat and messaging Mobile-first guest journey from check-in through checkout Built specifically for hospitality workflows and smaller hotel teams 2. Mews Mews is a cloud-native PMS popular with boutique hotels and lifestyle brands because of its modern approach to operating systems. The platform offers automation and self-service experiences, helping hotels modernize front desk operations and reduce manual work. Pros of Mews: Strong automation and self-service tools Open API ecosystem with extensive integrations via Mews Marketplace Cons of Mews: Advanced features may require additional modules Complex configuration and onboarding setup Reporting customization can be limited 3. Cloudbeds Cloudbeds is an all-in-one hospitality platform that combines property management, booking tools and channel management into a single system. It’s used by independent hotels looking for a centralized operational platform. Pros of Cloudbeds: Integrated channel manager and booking engine User-friendly dashboard for smaller properties Cons of Cloudbeds: Some automation tools require higher-tier plans Limited customization for complex operations Customer support response times may vary 4. Stayntouch Stayntouch is a mobile-first PMS designed to streamline hotel operations and guest experiences. Its flexible platform is especially popular with boutique and lifestyle hotels that want contactless service and multi-property management. Pros of Stayntouch: Mobile-friendly interface for staff and guests Contactless check-in and guest engagement tools Cons of Stayntouch: Smaller integration marketplace than some competitors Reporting tools may lack depth for advanced users Some features require third-party add-ons 5. Hotelogix Hotelogix is a cloud-based hotel management platform designed for independent hotels and small hotel groups. It focuses on simplifying reservations, front desk operations and housekeeping management. Pros of Hotelogix: Affordable pricing for smaller properties Multi-property management support Cons of Hotelogix: User interface feels dated compared to newer platforms Certain guest automation features, such as mobile check-in and guest messaging, require add-ons Some users report mobile app and sync gaps 6. RMS Cloud RMS Cloud offers hotels, resorts and serviced apartments a PMS combined with channel management and housekeeping tools. The platform emphasizes operational visibility and centralized management. Pros of RMS Cloud: Strong reservation and housekeeping management Flexible configuration options Cons of RMS Cloud: Interface can feel complex for smaller teams Setup and onboarding may take time Reporting configurations are less flexible than other parts of the platform 7. Little Hotelier Little Hotelier, which is part of the wider SiteMinder ecosystem, is designed specifically for small independent hotels, inns and bed-and-breakfast properties. It has a simplified feature set that makes it approachable for hotels with small operational teams, while offering PMS, channel manager and booking engine capabilities. Pros of Little Hotelier: Easy setup and intuitive interface Built specifically for small independent properties Cons of Little Hotelier: Limited scalability for growing hotel groups Fewer advanced guest engagement tools Guest engagement tools require a pro-level add-on 8. RoomRaccoon RoomRaccoon combines PMS functionality with booking, payments and channel management tools in one platform focused on independent hotels. It’s particularly popular in Europe, where the business originated. Pros of RoomRaccoon: Built-in upselling and payment tools Strong automation for reservations and invoicing Cons of RoomRaccoon: Limited enterprise-level reporting capabilities Some integrations are region-specific Customer support experiences can vary 9. Oracle OPERA Cloud Oracle OPERA Cloud is a widely used enterprise hospitality platform that supports hotels of all sizes. While powerful, it’s better suited for larger operations with more complex infrastructure needs. Pros of Oracle OPERA Cloud: Extensive enterprise functionality Strong reporting and operational controls Cons of Oracle OPERA Cloud: Higher complexity than many boutique hotels require Longer onboarding and training process Can be expensive for smaller independent properties 10. ThinkReservations ThinkReservations is a reservation and property management platform tailored for boutique hotels, vacation rentals and bed-and-breakfasts. The software manages operations and digital presence (e.g. a website builder). Pros of ThinkReservations: Easy-to-use booking and reservation tools Strong customer support reputation Cons of ThinkReservations: Closed ecosystem without an open API marketplace Fewer integrations than larger PMS platforms Best suited for smaller properties 11. Maestro PMS Maestro PMS is a hospitality management platform designed for independent hotels, resorts and multi-property groups, with a cloud or on-premise option. It includes a variety of operational tools, including specialized services like golf operations. Pros of Maestro PMS: Strong multi-property management features Customizable workflows and operational tools Cons of Maestro PMS: Interface may feel outdated to some users Steeper learning curve during onboarding More complex internal troubleshooting due to feature density Benefits of Implementing the Right Hotel Management Software Boutique hoteliers are really feeling the squeeze of operational demands and growing guest expectations right now. According to the American Hotel and Lodging Association's latest data, operating costs are the biggest demand. Hotels also need to convince guests to stay longer — half of all travelers now want to hotel hop, according to Expedia's Unpack '26 report. For property managers, the right hotel management software is a powerful tool for staying flexible in a changing hospitality landscape. Here’s how: It Increases Operational Efficiency without Expanding Staff Boutique staff members are the ultimate jacks-of-all-trades. On any given shift, a lean independent team isn't just managing the front desk, but also acting as local concierges, coordinating housekeeping and arranging next week’s theme night. That’s where modern hotel management software makes a real difference. It acts as a force multiplier, automating repetitive administrative work so they can deliver the hospitality. Automation tools like mobile check-in, AI-powered guest messaging and digital payments reduce bottlenecks while improving response times for guests. This becomes especially valuable during peak arrival periods when teams are stretched thin and guest expectations remain high. Key operational efficiency benefits include: Faster workflows that improve hotel productivity Reduced front desk workload through automation Streamlined housekeeping and guest communication processes Fewer manual errors and repetitive administrative tasks It Improves Guest Satisfaction Through Personalization Accor has found that 25% of travelers now expect to begin their search with a feeling or “vibe.” Convenience, speed and personalized service from the moment they book tend to be part of that expectation; something that independent hotels stand for, after all. Boutique hotel management software allows you to create those tailored guest experiences through automated communication, personalized offers and mobile-first interactions. Features like AI-powered messaging, mobile check-in and digital guest engagement tools allow hotels to respond faster while maintaining a more personal experience. This combination of convenience and customization improves the modern boutique guest journey and guest satisfaction. The ways hotel software improves the guest experience include: Personalized guest messaging before, during and after the stay Faster service through automated communication tools Mobile-first experiences that improve guest satisfaction Tailored upsell offers based on guest preferences and stay details It Drives More Direct Revenue The right hotel management software should fit like a glove. That means all the ways a property generates revenue, from rooms to rounds of golf, are supported. The best software also creates new revenue opportunities throughout the guest journey with automated upsells, AI-powered booking assistance and direct communication tools. For boutique hotels, this is where guest engagement functionality shines by offering room upgrades, late checkout, dining add-ons and personalized packages at the right moment in the guest journey. By automating these touchpoints, you increase conversion opportunities without any extra work. Its revenue-driving advantages include: Automated upsell campaigns that generate ancillary revenue AI tools that support direct bookings and guest communication Personalized offers that increase hotel software revenue opportunities Reduced operational inefficiencies that impact profitability It Delivers Clear Operational Visibility and Reporting Independent properties rely on hyper-targeted guest segmentation, local market agility and seamless execution to protect their profitability. If a repeat, high-value guest’s room preference is buried in an unread spreadsheet, your brand reputation takes a hit. Modern hotel management software eliminates blind spots by centralizing data so teams can make faster, more informed decisions without relying on disconnected systems or manual spreadsheets. Using centralized dashboards and real-time reporting makes it a cinch to monitor guest communication trends, operational bottlenecks, occupancy patterns and revenue performance. Because you have all this information right at your fingertips, you can more easily identify opportunities for improvement and maintain your service standards. Operational reporting benefits include: Real-time visibility into hotel performance and guest activity Centralized dashboards for operations and revenue tracking Better forecasting and staffing insights Faster decision-making backed by operational data Features of Effective Boutique Hotel Management Software From rustic vineyard retreats to ultra-minimalist urban lofts, there is a wide range of boutique hotels. However, the best ones share a common set of operational, guest-facing and technical competencies. An effective boutique hotel management system simplifies workflows, improves guest engagement and supports long-term growth without adding workload. Combine the following features to maximize daily efficiency, secure margins and protect staff bandwidth. Core Operations Capabilities The operational foundation piece requires an engine that matches your property's physical footprint, staffing scale and goals. A 15-room inn could suffocate its daily operations with an enterprise tool, and a multi-property collection would quickly stall the reservation management of a lightweight B&B tool. A management tool’s core capabilities shouldn't force you to change how you run your hotel; they should mirror your operational rhythm, automating the heavy administrative lifting so your team can focus on growth. To build a flawless operational foundation, independent hoteliers must prioritize these non-negotiable core pillars: Front Desk Management : Streamline check-in, checkout, room assignments and guest requests from a centralized dashboard. Housekeeping and Maintenance : Coordinate cleaning schedules, maintenance requests and staff workflows to better manage room cleanliness and room readiness. Billing and Accounting: Simplify invoicing, folio management and secure payment processing workflows. Reporting and Analytics: Access real-time operational and revenue insights to support faster decision-making. Process Automation : Reduce manual tasks with automated workflows for guest communication, payments and operational updates. Guest Experience Enhancements Once your operational foundation is solid, you can more easily build the guest journey on top. Because unique experiences are the lifeblood of boutique hotels, this layer must be tightly integrated with your core system to create a seamless, one-of-a-kind journey for guests without adding administrative strain on your team. To meet modern traveler expectations for instant, mobile-first convenience while preserving your signature human touch, prioritize tools that deliver: Engagement and Personalization : Create tailored guest experiences through personalized messaging, preferences and targeted offers. Mobile Accessibility: Give guests mobile-friendly options for check-in, room access, payments and communication. Upselling and Ancillary Revenue : Increase revenue beyond room rates with automated upgrades, add-ons and dynamic pricing opportunities. Integrated Communication: Centralize guest conversations across channels with tools like guest messaging . Technology and Infrastructure Last but not least is your infrastructure backbone — the technical foundation that future-proofs your investment. Your operational base and guest journey components need a modern, secure, easy-to-deploy architecture that can grow with your business goals. Choosing a cloud-first infrastructure means your lean team can securely manage the property from anywhere, eliminating the headache of outdated local servers and manual software updates. Look for software built with: Cloud-Based Infrastructure: Access hotel operations securely from any device without relying on on-premise servers. Third-Party Integrations: Easily connect with relevant platforms such as CRMs, payment providers and other hospitality tools. User-Friendly Interface: Reduce training time with intuitive dashboards and simplified workflows for hotel staff. Scalability: Support future growth across additional rooms, properties or operational needs without replacing systems. How to Select the Best Boutique Hotel Software for Your Property There’s a lot to consider when choosing your next technology platform, but you’ll want to focus on usability, flexibility, integration and long-term cost. Think of it as an accelerator for your business. The ideal system should reduce repetitive manual tasks, improve the guest experience and fit the size and scale of your property without overwhelming your team. By putting your top candidates through these five strategic steps, you can confidently choose a platform that supports your vision: 1. Identify Your Operational Priorities Every boutique hotel operates differently, which means the best software choice depends heavily on your property’s operational goals. Some hotels prioritize faster check-in experiences and guest communication, while others focus on housekeeping coordination, direct bookings or ancillary revenue opportunities. Before evaluating vendors, identify the biggest operational bottlenecks your team faces today. Understanding where staff spends the most time and where guest friction occurs most often makes it easier to prioritize the features that will have the biggest impact. Questions to consider include: Which operational tasks consume the most staff time? Where do guests experience the most friction? Which manual processes should be automated first? What revenue opportunities are currently being missed? 2. Evaluate Ease of Use for Lean Teams If it’s hard to understand, it won't work. Software that requires extensive onboarding or has complex workflows can hinder adoption and increase operational strain, particularly in boutique hotels with smaller teams handling multiple responsibilities. Look for platforms with intuitive dashboards, mobile accessibility and simplified workflows that staff can learn quickly. The best hotel software for boutique hotels features a user-friendly interface that reduces time spent on troubleshooting or employee training. Important usability factors include: Intuitive interface design Minimal onboarding and training requirements Mobile-friendly functionality for staff and guests Easy access to support and troubleshooting resources 3. Assess Integration Capabilities Your tools are only as powerful as their ability to talk to one another. Watch out for fragmented technology that forces your team into the frustrating role of human “middleware” — manually copy-pasting reservation numbers, duplicating billing entry tasks and trying to piece together guest histories across disconnected screens — while your guest watches. When evaluating software, prioritize platforms that integrate with your existing PMS, CRM, payment providers or guest engagement tools. Strong integrations create a unified tech stack and improve operational visibility across departments. Key integrations to evaluate include: PMS and reservation systems Payment and billing platforms CRM and guest profile tools Communication and messaging systems 4. Consider Total Cost of Ownership Is it worth it? Remember, software costs extend beyond the initial subscription price. Boutique hotels should evaluate onboarding fees, integration costs, support services and long-term scalability when comparing platforms. A lower-cost solution may appear attractive up front but create additional expenses later through limited functionality, operational inefficiencies or expensive add-ons. Evaluating total value rather than just monthly pricing leads to better long-term investment decisions. Cost considerations should include: Subscription and licensing fees Implementation and onboarding costs Integration and customization expenses Ongoing support and scalability pricing 5. Look for Boutique-Specific Functionality Go for a tailored product. Many enterprise hotel systems are designed primarily for large brands and complex corporate operations. Boutique hotels usually get more out of software that was made for smaller teams, personalized service models and flexible guest experiences. Consider software that builds around the reality of a location, like at this hotel that is so remote it can only be reached by train. Its software now arranges pick-ups for guests as part of mobile check-in. To achieve customization, look for platforms that prioritize guest engagement, mobile-first experiences and operational automation for independent hotels. Hospitality-specific AI, personalized communication tools and streamlined workflows are especially valuable for boutique properties competing on service quality and efficiency. Boutique-focused capabilities may include: Mobile check-in and contactless guest experiences Personalized guest communication tools Automated upselling and ancillary revenue features Hospitality-specific AI and workflow automation Enhance Boutique Hotel Operations with Technology from Canary Boutique hotels need technology that simplifies operations without sacrificing the personalized service that sets their properties apart. Canary’s guest management system gives independent hotels an all-in-one platform to automate workflows, improve guest communication and create seamless digital experiences across the entire guest journey. Built specifically for hospitality, Canary combines AI-powered guest engagement with operational automation to help smaller teams work more efficiently while delivering high-touch service. From mobile check-in and AI Guest Messaging to upsells and Smart Checkout, Canary modernizes boutique hotels’ operations, reduces front desk workload and unlocks new revenue opportunities. Key Canary features for boutique hotels include: Mobile Check-In and Smart Checkout for faster arrivals and departures AI-powered Guest Messaging across text, webchat and voice Automated upselling tools that increase ancillary revenue Mobile Key integrations for contactless guest access Hospitality-specific AI workflows designed for hotel operations Centralized guest communication and operational visibility Digital Compendium tools that improve on-property engagement Streamlined payment and authorization workflows Book a demo today and see how Canary's boutique hotel management software can streamline your operations and deliver a better guest experience. ‍

title: Amazon MSK now supports configuring custom domain names for MSK Provisioned clusters
summary: Discover more about what's new at AWS with Amazon MSK now supports configuring custom domain names for MSK Provisioned clusters
body_text: You can now easily configure custom domain names on Amazon MSK Provisioned clusters, on either ZooKeeper or KRaft mode for metadata management. This capability helps client applications maintain the same connection endpoints, simplifying cluster migrations, disaster recovery failovers, and scaling operations without reconfiguration. Previously, customers configured custom domain names manually on each broker. Additionally, on KRaft-based clusters, customers could not configure custom domain names. With this launch, you can now easily define a custom domain once at the cluster level, and Amazon MSK automatically applies it to every broker in the cluster, eliminating the need to configure each broker individually. The configuration persists through scaling operations and works identically on both ZooKeeper and KRaft-based clusters. This is particularly useful for customers who route traffic through Network Load Balancers, require persistent endpoints across cluster operations, or must adhere to organizational naming conventions for security and compliance. You can configure custom domain names on all new and existing MSK Provisioned clusters, in all AWS Regions where Amazon MSK Provisioned is available, at no additional cost. To learn more, see the Amazon MSK Developer Guide .

title: AVITA Medical Reports Second Quarter Results, Raises 2026 Revenue Guidance, and Expects Fourth Quarter Cash Flow Breakeven
summary: VALENCIA, Calif., Aug. 06, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- AVITA Medical ®, Inc. (NASDAQ: RCEL, ASX: AVH), a leading therapeutic acute wound care company delivering transformative solutions (“AVITA Medical,” or the “Company”), today reported financial results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026.
body_text: AVITA Medical Reports Second Quarter Results, Raises 2026 Revenue Guidance, and Expects Fourth Quarter Cash Flow Breakeven August 6, 2026 PDF Version VALENCIA, Calif., Aug. 06, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- AVITA Medical®, Inc. (NASDAQ: RCEL, ASX: AVH), a leading therapeutic acute wound care company delivering transformative solutions (“AVITA Medical,” or the “Company”), today reported financial results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026. Second Quarter 2026 Financial Highlights Q2 net revenue grew 18% year over year and 13% sequentially quarter-over-quarter to a record $21.7 million Revenue growth driven by continued execution across the Company's key commercial portfolio, led by RECELL® and supported by increasing adoption of Cohealyx® and PermeaDerm®, and complemented by consistent international revenue Gross profit margin of 81.9%, an increase of 70 basis points year-over-year, reflecting the growth of RECELL alongside the expansion of the Company’s other product portfolio Operating expenses were $24.6 million, down 6% year-over-year demonstrating continued operating discipline while supporting commercial growth Net cash use improved to approximately $3.2 million, from $9.9 million in Q1 2026, with cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities at the end of the quarter of approximately $11.1 million Raised full-year 2026 net revenue guidance range to $86 million to $89 million, reflecting confidence in continued commercial execution The Company expects to reach cash flow breakeven in the fourth quarter 2026 Business Updates The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services released proposed calendar year 2027 Medicare payment updates for RECELL that, if adopted, would set national (as opposed to region-by-region) physician payment for the use of RECELL as well as increase hospital outpatient and ambulatory surgical center facility payment rates Expect to present PermeaDerm I study data in August Cary Vance, President and Chief Executive Officer of AVITA Medical, commented: “We delivered a strong second quarter, with revenue growing 18% year-over-year and 13% sequentially. As AVITA continues to expand utilization in the U.S. and build its presence in key international markets, our results reflect the strength of both our acute wound care portfolio and our commercial execution, led by RECELL and supported by Cohealyx and PermeaDerm. We are delivering this growth while maintaining a high gross margin and disciplined operating expenses and use of cash. Together, these results demonstrate that AVITA has evolved into a business capable of sustained, durable growth, giving us the confidence to raise our full-year revenue guidance and to announce our expectation to reach cash flow breakeven in the fourth quarter.” David O'Toole, Chief Financial Officer, commented: “During the second quarter, we maintained a disciplined approach to operating expenses while delivering record revenue and, as expected, a further reduction in net use of cash. As the business continues to scale, supported by sustained high gross margins, operating expense management, and improved timely customer cash collections, we expect to reach cash flow breakeven and to start generating cash in the fourth quarter of 2026.” Updated Financial Guidance Based on the Company’s second quarter performance, AVITA Medical is increasing its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to be in the range of $86 million to $89 million, from $80 million to $85 million, compared to $71.6 million of revenue in 2025, representing year-over-year growth in the range of 20% to 24%. AVITA Medical is also expecting to achieve cash flow breakeven in the fourth quarter of 2026. Second Quarter Financial Results Total revenue was approximately $21.7 million in the three months ended June 30, 2026, an increase of 18% compared to $18.4 million in the prior-year period. Revenue growth in the quarter was driven by continued execution across the Company's key commercial portfolio, led by RECELL and supported by Cohealyx and PermeaDerm. RECELL (Q2 revenue of $18.5 million, approximately 11% growth compared to Q1 2026) continued to drive the business, with sequential growth supported by increasing physician confidence following reimbursement stabilization and continued adoption of RECELL GO mini, which expanded utilization in smaller wounds. Cohealyx (Q2 revenue of $1.7 million, approximately 16% growth compared to Q1 2026) continued to build commercial momentum. Growth was further supported by favorable interim clinical data from the Company’s Cohealyx I clinical study reported in April demonstrating a faster time to skin grafting readiness than leading competitive products. PermeaDerm (Q2 revenue of $0.6 million, approximately 40% growth compared to Q1 2026) gained traction during the second quarter. PermeaDerm is a wound temporizer, providing clinicians with an alternative to allograft to temporarily stabilize and protect the wound before definitive closure. The Company's PermeaDerm I clinical study evaluating PermeaDerm as a clinically comparable, lower-cost alternative to allograft ​is expected in August. International (Q2 revenue of $0.9 million, approximately 26% growth compared to Q1 2026) continued to contribute consistent revenue from established international markets. Gross profit margin was 81.9%, compared to 81.2% in the prior-year period, despite the continued expansion of the Company’s product portfolio. The Company shares the average sales price for Cohealyx at 50%, and for PermeaDerm at 60%, which inevitably results in an overall decrease in gross margin percentage. RECELL-only gross margin was 86.0% for the quarter. Operating expenses were $24.6 million, down 6% or $1.5 million compared with $26.1 million in the prior-year period. The decrease primarily reflected continued execution of cost optimization initiatives and commercial restructuring actions implemented in 2025, including a $0.7 million reduction in sales and marketing expenses. General and administrative expenses decreased by $0.7 million while research and development expenses were flat with the prior-year period. The Company ended the quarter with approximately $11.1 million in cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities, compared with $14.3 million at the beginning of the quarter. The Company believes its current liquidity, together with expected operating improvements, provides capital to support execution of its commercial strategy and expected path to fourth-quarter cash flow breakeven. Under the Company's existing credit facility, an additional tranche of $10 million remains available upon achieving at least $85 million of trailing twelve-month net revenue in any month prior to March 31, 2027. Net loss improved to $7.7 million, or a loss of $0.25 per basic and diluted share, compared with a net loss of $9.9 million, or a loss of $0.38 per basic and diluted share, in the prior-year period. CMS Proposes 2027 Medicare Provider Reimbursement for RECELL In July, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (“CMS”) released the 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule (“PFS”), Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System (“OPPS”), and Ambulatory Surgical Center (“ASC”) proposed rules addressing Medicare payment for Skin Cell Suspension Autograft, the procedure performed using RECELL The proposed rules reflect the new Category I CPT code family, effective January 1, 2027, and include proposed national physician relative value units based on the American Medical Association-RVS Update Committee recommended valuation, as well as proposed increases to hospital outpatient and ASC facility payment rates. If finalized, RECELL physician payment would transition from the current regional Medicare Administrative Contractor contractor-priced methodology to a more transparent, nationally published physician valuation framework under the PFS. CMS is expected to issue final rules later this year, with implementation effective January 1, 2027. title: We Caught a North Korean Operative in a Hiring Pipeline. Here is What We Learned.
summary: When candidates never enter an office, your verification process is the only barrier to fraud.
body_text: The Case A U.S. Department of Defense contractor was hiring for a remote technical role. Two candidates made the shortlist. Strong resumes, solid qualifications, great interviews. By every traditional measure, both were excellent hires. There was one problem: they were the same person. Same face, same background on the video call. Different shirt, different name, different company. Had the applications gone to different recruiters, or been reviewed even a few days apart, no one would have noticed. When Alex's Fraud Detection Agent analyzed both candidates, one triggered 34 fraudulent signals. The other triggered 92. New email accounts, thin digital footprints, location data that didn't match. Synthetic identity patterns specifically designed to game the traditional interview process. Invisible to a human reviewer. Unmistakable to a system built to find it. The Threat Is Wider Than You Think Unfortunately this wasn't a one-off. This candidate was part of a network. In March, NBC News reported that threat intelligence firm Nisos had uncovered at least 20 North Korean operatives who had collectively applied to more than 160,000 jobs across the United States. Their motives range from intelligence gathering to earning U.S. salaries and routing money back to North Korea through intermediary bank accounts. But North Korean operatives represent the far end of a much wider spectrum. The more common version of this is happening in hiring pipelines every day: Candidates hiring proxy interviewers. Fabricating credentials. Building synthetic identities. Creating LinkedIn profiles last week to support resumes that claim ten years of experience. Where Traditional Hiring Breaks Down Remote hiring has made all of it even easier. When a candidate never walks into an office, the only thing standing between a fraudulent applicant and a job offer is whatever verification your process includes. Most processes don't include enough. Traditional background checks happen late, after recruiters have already spent hours screening and interviewing. They confirm that a Social Security number matches a name. They don't confirm that the person on your video call is the person behind that number. Catching Fraud Before the First Interview Alex's Fraud Detection works at the front of the pipeline. The moment a candidate is invited to interview, the system evaluates signals across email verification, phone analysis, LinkedIn validation, and indicators like disposable accounts, VOIP numbers, newly created profiles, fraud history. These are all flagged before a recruiter spends a single minute on the candidate. After the interview, a second layer cross-references IP addresses and identity signals against the candidate's claimed information. It's not a background check. It's the question that comes before a background check: is this person real? For the Department of Defense contractor, the answer was no. 92 times over. If your process can't catch the same person applying twice with a different shirt, it's worth asking what else it's missing. ‍ Learn more about Fraud Detection →

title: A Developer's Guide to Building on the Onchain AI Agent Stack | Quicknode
summary: Explore the onchain AI agent stack, from blockchain access and ERC-8004 identity to x402 payments, execution, and production infrastructure.
body_text: A Developer's Guide to Building on the Onchain AI Agent Stack Explore the onchain AI agent stack, from blockchain access and ERC-8004 identity to x402 payments, execution, and production infrastructure. Quicknode August 18, 2026 — 13 min read AI agents are everywhere today. McDonald's support bot, coding assistants, and seemingly every startup pitch in the last two years. Yet ask ten builders, or read ten articles ranking on page one of Google, and there will be ten different answers to "what is an AI agent?" and "how do AI agents actually work?". Why so? Universally, there's no exact definition. Yet everyone is convinced that everyone needs AI agents and that building one is easy. This piece breaks AI agents down to their atoms: what they actually are, how autonomy works, where blockchain fits, and how each piece of the stack works together. What are AI Agents, Actually? AI agents are software that observes its environment, uses reasoning and memory to decide what to do, and takes actions autonomously to achieve a goal. Every AI agent is built around four fundamental components: Goal: Defines the objective the agent is trying to accomplish. Observe: Gathers information from its environment through user input, APIs, databases, browsers, or other data sources. Reason: Uses model, memory, and available context to decide what should happen next. Act: Uses tools to initiate actions like send a request, write a file, execute code, make a transaction, or trigger another system. The goal sets the direction. Observe > Reason > Act forms the loop that continues until the goal is achieved or the agent reaches a stopping condition. The ability to act is what matters here. Without it, reasoning stays inside the model, which brings us to a huge confusion present online: agents vs models. AI Agents vs LLM Models An LLM provides the reasoning engine inside many AI agents. The "agent" emerges when reasoning is connected to memory, tools, workflows, and execution. Consider a task: Research the top 10 competitors in a market and compare their pricing. An LLM can suggest how to approach the task. An agent can actually carry it out: The cycle can repeat dozens of times. And this is exactly where AI agents go beyond just an LLM model. The model supplies reasoning. Tools provide capabilities. Infrastructure determines where those actions can happen. Access decides how autonomous (human-free) actions can be. Put another way, an LLM can tell an agent what it should do. The rest of the stack determines whether the agent can actually do it. And this is where today's agents begin to hit a boundary. AI Agents Hit the Autonomy Wall Most AI agents interact with the world through infrastructure built for humans. They use API keys created by developers, accounts registered by people, cloud services billed to companies, payment methods attached to those accounts, and permissions granted by administrators. The agent may decide to take an action, but the underlying ability to take that action often still belongs to someone else. This is the gap between an agent that can call tools and an agent that can operate independently. Greater autonomy requires more than better LLMs. Agents need ways to establish identity, control assets, exchange value, and execute actions without humans. That's where blockchain becomes interesting. Why Put AI Agents Onchain? Blockchain gives AI agents access to programmable primitives for ownership, identity, payments, execution, and shared state. It doesn't make an LLM autonomous by itself. Instead, it gives an agent new ways to interact with the world. Five primitives are particularly relevant: Together, these primitives change what an agent can do. An agent could hold funds, pay for a service, prove which identity it is acting through, interact with a smart contract, and leave a verifiable record of what happened. But none of this happens simply because an agent has a wallet. There is a stack of infrastructure sitting between the reasoning loop and the blockchain for those capabilities to work in practice. Let's take a look. What is the Onchain AI Agent Stack? The onchain AI agent stack is a set of infrastructure layers, spanning payment, identity, access, and coordination, that let AI agents act autonomously on blockchain. These layers come together to let an agent hold a wallet, prove identity, pay for resources, and execute transactions with limited to no human involvement. For this guide, the stack can be understood through three parts. These three parts form the architecture for the rest of this guide: Access > Identity > Discovery > Payments > Execution > Operations Each part depends on the one before it. Economic agency without access is a concept, not a capability. Operations without economic agency have nothing to operate. So, let's begin where the stack actually starts: getting the agent onto the chain in the first place. Giving AI Agents Blockchain Access Blockchain access gives an AI agent the ability to read onchain state and submit transactions. In practice, this usually starts with an RPC endpoint that connects the agent to a blockchain node. RPC works much like an API. The agent sends a request to a node and receives blockchain data in return. The same interface can broadcast signed transactions when the agent needs to act. That covers the two basic directions an agent needs: Read: Check balances, query smart contracts, inspect transactions, estimate gas, or retrieve the latest block. Write: Broadcast transfers, swaps, contract calls, or other signed transactions. Choosing the Right Blockchain Interface The interface depends on what the agent needs to observe. JSON-RPC over HTTP works for basic request-response tasks such as checking a balance or broadcasting a transaction. WebSockets maintain a persistent connection. They suit agents that need to watch new blocks, logs, or other state changes and react as they happen. gRPC is built for specialized workloads like high-throughput streaming of accounts, transactions, slots, and other real-time data. Quicknode provides these interfaces across 80+ chains and 130+ networks through a common API point . For latency-sensitive or high-volume workloads, Dedicated Clusters provide isolated infrastructure. Reacting to Onchain Events Reading the state and reacting to it are different problems. Polling works but wastes calls and misses anything between checks. This is why AI agents need a way to detect onchain events and respond to them. A trading agent, for example, cannot wait for a prompt before noticing a price change, transaction, or contract event. Quicknode provides two main ways to build these workflows: Streams delivers real-time and historical blockchain data to destinations such as webhooks and databases. It supports filtering, reorg handling, and reliable delivery for workflows where missing an event can affect execution. Webhooks sends event notifications through HTTP callbacks. It offers a simpler setup for workflows where best-effort delivery is sufficient. With access and event delivery sorted, let's tackle agentic identity, i.e., establishing which agent is doing the observing and acting. How AI Agents Get an Onchain Identity Onchain identity allows AI agents to be recognized and identified verifiably before any interaction or transaction happens. ERC-8004 provides this through onchain registries for identity, reputation, and validation. Registering costs one transaction. After that, any agent or service can look up the registration and decide whether to interact. Every agent gets: A reputation score that takes into account feedback volume, how many distinct counterparties left that feedback, and how often the agent's work got flagged or reversed. Validation attestation, i.e., an independent check on whether an agent actually did what it claimed*. Bonus: Read how ERC-8004 works , how it fares against OAuth, DIDs, and ENS, and more importantly, how to register and interact with other AI agents. *Not live on mainnet as of mid-August 2026. An agent can query these registries two ways using Quicknode: The ERC-8004 Explorer provides a human-readable interface for searching registered agents and inspecting their profiles, reputation, and activity. Applications can retrieve the same indexed data through the ERC-8004 REST API or JSON-RPC add-on . Developers that need direct access can query the underlying ERC-8004 registry contracts through Core RPC instead. Identity establishes who an agent is and how to discover other AI agents. The next question becomes economic: how can AI agents transact with each other? How AI Agents Pay Autonomously Autonomous payments let AI agents purchase APIs, data, compute, and other services without relying on a human. Two protocols do this today: x402 and MPP. x402: Pay Per Request x402 lets an agent pay for an HTTP resource as part of the request itself. When the agent requests a paid resource, the server returns 402 Payment Required with the price, network, token, and payment instructions. The agent signs the payment, retries the request with the authorization attached, and receives the resource once payment is verified. A facilitator can handle verification and onchain settlement for the server. Bonus: YouTube tutorial on how to use x402 to build content paywalls . This works well for discrete purchases such as API calls, data queries, or compute jobs. MPP: Pay for Ongoing Access Machine Payments Protocol (MPP) lets agents establish paid sessions for services that involve repeated or ongoing interactions. Instead of treating every request as a separate purchase, payment and access can persist across a longer session. This fits services such as persistent infrastructure or long-running workloads, where repeatedly negotiating a new payment for every request is unnecessary. Bonus: Learn how to use MPP to access blockchain data via Quicknode. The distinction is practical: x402 prices the request; MPP can price the relationship that continues across requests. Quicknode Enables Both x402 and MPP Quicknode makes both payment models usable against its own infrastructure. x402 access lets a wallet consume Quicknode endpoints without creating an account or API key, with pay-per-request, nanopayment, and prepaid credit-drawdown models across JSON-RPC, REST, gRPC-Web, and WebSocket. MPP access supports both one-off charges and reusable payment sessions; sessions open a payment channel once, then use signed vouchers for subsequent requests before final onchain settlement. Both protocols share one free-tier bucket, i.e., 1 million API credits a month per wallet, and both can query any of Quicknode's supported chains regardless of which network the payment settles on. Now, an AI agent has decided what to do and has the economic ability to do it. How does that decision become an onchain transaction? How AI Agents Execute Onchain Actions Onchain execution turns an agent's decision into a blockchain transaction. An agent might decide to transfer USDC, execute a swap, claim a position, or call a smart contract. This decision is taken at the reasoning layer. But transaction execution infrastructure handles how that action reaches the blockchain. From Decision to Transaction Execution starts by translating an agent's intent into a valid transaction. That means identifying the contract and method, preparing parameters, estimating fees, and constructing the transaction in the format expected by the target chain. Signing is the critical boundary. Once signed, the transaction can be broadcast through Quicknode Core RPC . Preparing Assets Before Execution Agents will not always hold the asset required for the next action. A payment may require USDC while the wallet holds ETH. A protocol interaction may require another token entirely. Quicknode's Swap API provides a programmatic way to fetch routes and prepare swaps without requiring the agent to integrate with individual DEXs. That makes asset routing another callable capability inside the workflow: Check balance > Get swap route > Execute swap > Confirm balance > Continue task At this point, the agent can access the blockchain state, establish an identity, pay for resources, and execute transactions. The remaining challenge is operational: keeping those capabilities available, reliable, and constrained while the agent runs without constant human supervision. Managing AI Agent Infrastructure in Production Production AI agents need infrastructure that stays available, reacts to changing workloads, discovers and interacts with the right tools, and monitors and limits access. Earlier layers give an agent capabilities. The production layer determines whether those capabilities can run continuously without turning every infrastructure change into a human task. Letting Agents Manage Their Own Infrastructure Quicknode's Admin API exposes infrastructure management programmatically. This creates a path for approved agent workflows to provision and manage resources through APIs. Managing Infrastructure in Natural Language Quicknode also enables access to the same infrastructure through an MCP server so that an agent, or the developer working alongside one, can create an endpoint, check usage, or update a rate limit by asking for it in plain language instead of writing API calls by hand. Agent-facing resources such as Blockchain Skills and llms.txt complement this layer by making documentation and blockchain knowledge easier for agents to consume. Constraining What an Agent Can Do Production autonomy should have explicit boundaries. An agent only needs access to the networks, methods, resources, and credentials required for its task. Quicknode provides controls such as JWT authentication , IP allowlisting , method-specific rate limits , and role-based access control (RBAC) . This creates bounded autonomy: enough authority for an agent to operate independently, without turning a compromised prompt or incorrect decision into unrestricted infrastructure or asset access. With that, the stack closes its loop. Intelligence determines what should happen; the surrounding infrastructure determines what an agent can observe, pay for, execute, and operate safely over time. AI Agents May Be Blockchain's Most Natural Users For more than a decade, blockchain applications have largely been designed around humans. Today, when we zoom out and look at portable identity, programmable money, and execution without intermediaries, we realize agents are the first class of economic actors blockchain's original design assumptions were built for. Trustless, because there's no legal recourse between two pieces of software. Programmable, because a human isn't reading the terms. Permissionless, because nobody's there to approve the application. Knowing this, we look optimistically toward a future where the primary user of blockchain is AI agents. FAQs: Frequently Asked Questions 1. Does every AI agent need blockchain infrastructure? No. Blockchain becomes useful when agents need onchain state, programmable assets, payments, portable identity, or execution across independent systems. 2. What can AI agents actually do onchain? Agents can monitor blockchain activity, query contracts, manage assets, make payments, execute transactions, and trigger workflows based on onchain events. 3. Can an AI agent lose money it controls? Yes. A wallet an agent controls has no fraud protection, no chargebacks, and no bank to call if something goes wrong. 4. What is the difference between an onchain AI agent and a trading bot? Trading bots automate predefined market strategies. AI agents can reason, select tools, adapt workflows, and perform broader onchain tasks. 5. Can existing AI agents be made onchain? Yes. Existing agents can add blockchain capabilities through RPC APIs, wallets, payment protocols, identity standards, and transaction tools. 6. Can two AI agents transact without any humans involved? Yes. End-to-end discovery, payment, and execution can all happen without a person approving each step. 7. How is an onchain identity different from an OAuth token? An OAuth token is issued and revoked by one platform. Onchain identity is self-owned and portable across any of them.
